questions.q: What does `SELECT SUM(invoice_amount) FROM ap_invoices_all;` return, with no GROUP BY?
options: One row per invoice, with a running total
Exactly one row — the grand total across every row the query sees
One row per supplier
An error, since SUM requires GROUP BY
questions.explain: Without GROUP BY, an aggregate function like SUM collapses the entire result into a single row.

options: The sum of a numeric column
The number of distinct values in a column
The number of NULL values only
The number of rows
questions.explain: COUNT(*) counts rows, regardless of what values any particular column holds.

questions.q: Why does `SELECT vendor_id, invoice_num, SUM(invoice_amount) FROM ap_invoices_all GROUP BY vendor_id;` produce an error?
options: invoice_num is neither wrapped in an aggregate function nor listed in GROUP BY, so there's no single value to show per group
SUM cannot be used with GROUP BY
vendor_id must always be aggregated
GROUP BY can only be used with exactly one column total
questions.explain: Once rows are grouped by vendor_id, invoice_num varies within each group, so Oracle cannot resolve a single value for it per group.

questions.q: What are the three conceptual steps GROUP BY performs?
options: Sort, filter, limit
Join, filter, sort
Split rows into groups, aggregate within each group, combine into one row per group
Delete, insert, update
questions.explain: GROUP BY splits rows by the grouping column(s), aggregates separately within each group, then combines the results into one row per group.

questions.q: In `SELECT i.invoice_num, SUM(ip.amount) AS total_paid FROM ap_invoices_all i INNER JOIN ap_invoice_payments_all ip ON ip.invoice_id = i.invoice_id GROUP BY i.invoice_num;`, what problem does GROUP BY solve?
options: It removes the need for an INNER JOIN
It collapses the multiple rows per invoice (one per check) from Lesson 7's join back into one row per invoice, with payments totaled
It sorts invoices by amount
It filters out invoices with no payments
questions.explain: The join alone can return multiple rows per invoice; GROUP BY with SUM folds those back into one row per invoice, totaling all payments applied.
